Project_Name: Alligator Lake Coastal Dune Lake Hydrologic Restoration
Project_Description: The project reduced pollution and hydrologic degradation to coastal waters within the Choctawhatchee Bay Watershed by removing culverts under County Road 30A that were deteriorating and/or in disrepair, acting as barriers separating the north and south portions of Alligator Lake rather than allowing the exchange of fresh and Gulf waters. The culverts acted as barriers to fish and wildlife and reduced water and sediment exchange. A bridge was constructed across Alligator Lake to help restore tidal exchange and remove barriers to fish and wildlife movements.  Specifically, the project included:  • Construction of a spanning bridge across Alligator Lake to replace culverts that were deteriorating and/or in disrepair; • Continued water quality sampling under an existing monitoring program. The project helped to restore the connection and circulation of the lake and improved the lake community and adjacent ecosystems, improved water quality in the lake, and enhanced fish and wildlife habitat. The project directly improved water quality in watersheds injured by the Deepwater Horizon oil spill by restoring hydrologic connections between the coastal and freshwater portions of Alligator Lake and enhancing coastal habitats. By replacing culverts in disrepair with a bridge, hydrologic connectivity was restored, resulting in improved water quality, water flows, and subsequent benefits to fish and wildlife. The project developed and implemented management actions to improve water quality in Alligator Lake and the Choctawhatchee Bay watershed by removing physical barriers from the lake. Project_Name: Beach and Dune Habitat Protection at Gulf Islands National Seashore
Project_Description: The project will protect beach-dune habitat and associated wildlife in the Perdido Key, Fort Pickens, and Santa Rosa areas at Gulf Islands National Seashore (GUIS) from three different threats: 1) human disturbance; 2) vehicle collisions on paved roads; and 3) predators. The project will last approximately five years. Specifically, this project will: 1) identify sensitive areas and use both temporary symbolic fencing and permanent post-and-rope fencing to close those areas to protect habitat, wildlife, and bird nests, and to prevent dune trampling; 2) if feasible, establish wildlife viewing areas at the edge of major bird colonies; 3) educate visitors on habitats and wildlife (including breeding birds) with public outreach materials provided at the entrance stations, such as score cards of hatches and mortality; 4) set up temporary signage and speed bumps and establish law enforcement patrols to monitor and control speeding vehicles and reduce vehicle collisions with wildlife; 5) implement predator management techniques such as perch deterrents and enclosures around bird and turtle nests; 6) survey animal burrows, bird nests, and colonies for predator activity and human disturbance; and 7) monitor bird nest success and fledging rates. This information will provide insights into causes of mortality and allow for adaptive management throughout the project by identifying the most effective closure areas and protection methods. The project is being extended another four years (through 2028) with additional funding received in 2024 from the Florida Trustee Implementation Group (TIG).

Project_Name: Big Bend Oyster Restoration
Project_Description:
Since the 1980’s, oyster reef habitat has declined precipitously in Florida’s Big Bend region of the Gulf of Mexico. To mitigate these declines, this oyster restoration project incorporated two new techniques in oyster restoration: (1) use of bagged building blocks of living oysters transplanted to create instant living reefs that are resilient to wave action, and (2) designing reefs to capture and protect extant oyster spat and increase growth and survival by enhancing water flow around reef structure in a way that allows built reefs to naturally expand.

The restoration project established stable substrate along 25 km of shoreline and used donated, bagged live oysters to boost oyster recruitment. Clean limerock boulders established a hard substrate over existing eroded sand bars and each site was lined with the oyster bags. 

The restoration of reefs in this pilot project suggests that long term resilience can be built into oyster reefs by the addition of hardened surface and durable substrate and that the established artificial reefs have positive effects on erosion, water flow, water quality, and wildlife.

Project_Name: Carpenter Creek Hydrologic Restoration and Stormwater Improvements
Project_Description:
The project will retrofit existing stormwater management systems and install additional stormwater infrastructure to provide additional water treatment, and thereby improve water quality in the Pensacola Bay watershed. The project will implement recommendations in the Carpenter Creek Watershed Master Plan, which included proposed sites and activities for stream restoration and stormwater treatment activities. Specifically, the project will:
• Restore 1,540 linear feet of Robins Ridge Stream and construct two detention ponds. The stream restoration will provide the drainage corridor a larger floodplain/wetland area to stabilize the stream channel, preventing erosion and reducing downstream sediment loads. A bottomland meander belt and headwater channel will be contoured through the bottomland forest (by moving/removing sediment). Native vegetation will be planted along the restored meander belt for stabilization.
• Install multiple stormwater filtering structures containing sediment settling chambers to capture and treat stormwater in drainageways near Coronet Drive. The structures will remove nitrogen, phosphorus, and suspended solids.
• Enhance existing stormwater ponds by installing bio-sorption activated media (BAM) stormwater infrastructure at three dry retention ponds near Cardinal Cove to reduce pollution influx into Carpenter Creek and remove energy from the system during heavy rainfall events.

The Carpenter Creek watershed is highly urbanized and developed with residential, commercial, and industrial areas. The high degree of impervious surfaces, relatively well-drained soils, and presence of multiple pollutant sources contribute to water quality impairment within the watershed. Water quality assessment results indicated that total phosphorus, fecal indicator bacteria, and dissolved oxygen are the major impairment concerns. The Pensacola Bay SWIM Plan and the Carpenter Creek Watershed Master Plan note that the implementation of best management practices (BMPs) for the urban watershed is needed for Carpenter Creek. The plans also note that restoration of the stream’s natural sinuosity would assist with the assimilation of urban waste loads and attenuate floodwaters bringing sediment to Bayou Texar.

The project will reduce pollutant loading and hydrologic degradation in the watershed, which flows into coastal waters. The restored floodplain area will improve the bottomland forest habitat and provide for species that depend on these habitats, stabilize soils, and reduce erosion and sediment loading into Carpenter Creek.

Project_Description: The project will employ four strategies (reduce human disturbance, improve habitat quality, reduce predation, and improve regulatory coordination) to increase populations of black skimmer, least tern, American oystercatcher, Wilson’s plover, and snowy plover. Project_Name: Gasparilla Sound Scallop Restoration
Project_Description: Gasparilla Sound is part of the Gasparilla Sound/Charlotte Harbor Aquatic Preserve and is managed to protect and restore submerged habitats, including seagrass, fish and shellfish. Bay scallop populations declined in the 1960s, primarily due to over harvest. Recovery of bay scallop populations requires adequate sources of larvae, especially following red tide events. Over 3 million bay scallop larvae, collected from nearshore waters in the Florida Panhandle, were released into Gasparilla Sound over healthy seagrass beds just prior to the stage in their life cycle where they settle onto the seagrass and develop into juvenile scallops. The purpose of the larval release was to provide adequate numbers of juvenile scallops to grow to adulthood and spawn the following fall in Gasparilla Sound. Monitoring of adult populations and next year’s recruitment of larvae is planned. The project involved local, state and regional agencies, as well as volunteers.
Habitat_Description: Gasparilla Sound (approximately 11,000 acres) is located in Lee County between the Cape Haze Peninsula and Gasparilla Island. Gasparilla Sound is connected to the Gulf of Mexico through Gasparilla Pass to the north and Boca Grande Pass to the south. It is part of the Gasparilla Sound/Charlotte Harbor Aquatic Preserve. It is a shallow healthy estuary surrounded by mangrove shoreline with little development and supports over 7,000 acres of seagrasses including turtle grass, shoal grass and manatee grass. The submerged habitats support a great diversity of fish, shellfish, invertebrates and marine mammals including oyster, clams, shrimp, mangrove snapper, snook, dolphins and manatees. Historically, bay scallops were abundant in Gasparilla Sound, but populations declined dramatically after the 1960s due primarily to over harvesting. Seagrass and water quality conditions are adequate to support bay scallop populations, but sources of larvae are limited and red tide adversely impacts fledgling populations.

Project_Name: Indian River Lagoon Impoundment Reconnection and Restoration
Project_Description: The St. John River Water Management District worked with the Brevard County Mosquito Control District and the Merritt Island National Wildlife Refuge to install culverts to enhance fish habitat in Brevard County, FL.  At the Sykes Creek Impoundments (C-2 North and C-2 South), which comprise nearly 2,015 acres of wetland, 17 culverts were installed to recreate flow where natural creek mouths previously existed and provide fish with access to habitat.  Work began on this component in September of 2015, restoring 1,289 acres.  The balance of acreage was completed in the fall of 2015.  Additional work was implemented in other impoundments within the Merritt Island National Wildlife Refuge to address subsidence. Subsidence has reduced sediment levels to elevations too low to support marsh grass or mangrove habitat.  This component of the project was implemented first as a pilot project to evaluate a variety of methods to bring subsided areas up to an appropriate elevation to support vegetation typical of wetlands in the area.  The pilot effort was completed in the spring of 2016.  Project results led to implementation of an expanded effort in the fall of 2016/winter of 2017.  Final planting was completed December 2017.

Project_Name: Indian River Lagoon Shoreline Restoration Project
Project_Description: This project restored mangrove habitat through community based education and hands on planting activities. This was addressed in two parts; the establishment, maintenance and monitoring of new and existing shoreline restoration sites was completed; and promotion of the project and awareness about the lagoon’s ecosystem through outreach and service learning was conducted. The program relies heavily on volunteer support with all aspects of the project, including assisting with monitoring, planting events, and maintenance at the Coastal Wetland Plant Nursery. The IRL SRP, currently managed by the FDEPand funded by the St. Johns Water Management District District and the Indian River Lagoon National Estuary Program, aims to re-establish fringing mangrove habitat along IRL shorelines while fostering community involvement and stewardship. Mangrove habitat along the shorelines of the Indian River Lagoon (IRL) has been in decline since the mid 1900’s. Mangroves are critical to the Indian River Lagoon ecosystem because they not only help to stabilize the shorelines, but they also serve as a nursery and safe haven for juvenile fish along with many other species native to the lagoon. The project was started in 1995 through the Environmental Learning Center (ELC), until 2008 when it was transferred to the Florida Department of Environmental Protection’s Office of Coastal and Aquatic Managed Areas (FDEP CAMA) Indian River Lagoon Aquatic Preserves Field Office. The project boundary extends from SR 528 in Brevard County to Jupiter Inlet in Palm Beach County.

Project_Name: J. N. Ding Darling National Wildlife Refuge Invasive Vegetation Control
Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 6,406 acre J.N. “Ding” Darling National Wildlife Refuge managed by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service. A large area of the refuge (2,619 acres) is designated as a Wilderness Area with limited access. Habitat restoration activities focus on prescribed fire, removal of invasive exotic and native vegetation and hydrologic restoration to restore the diversity of natural habitats throughout the refuge ridge and swale system. The habitat restoration projects improve wildlife habitat within refuge wetlands, as well as protect submerged seagrass habitats in the adjacent estuary. FY13 habitat restoration activities completed included 280 acres of invasive vegetation removal of Brazilian Pepper, Rosary Pea, Air potato and other species, as well as trail and road maintenance.
Habitat_Description: The J. N. “Ding” Darling National Wildlife Refuge (6,406 acres) is managed by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service. The refuge is located in western Lee County on Sanibel Island adjacent to Pine Island Sound Aquatic Preserve. One third of the refuge (2,619 acres) is designated as Wilderness Area. The refuge is a series of ridge and swales made up of several habitat types including estuarine habitat with open water, seagrass beds, mud flats and mangrove islands and interior freshwater habitats with open water ponds and spartina saltmarsh in the swales and West Indian hardwood hammocks on the ridges. Two brackish water impoundments totaling 800 acres are used extensively by wading birds and other water birds. The refuge has a large diversity of species. Several threatened and endangered species benefit from the habitats including eastern indigo snakes, American alligators, American crocodiles, wood storks, Florida manatees, Atlantic loggerhead sea turtles, Atlantic green sea turtles, hawksbill sea turtles, Kemp’s Ridley sea turtles, leatherback sea turtles, piping plovers, and smalltooth sawfish. Approximately 272 bird species have been identified utilizing refuge habitats, as well as 60 species of reptiles and amphibians, 33 species of mammals, and 102 species of fish.

Project_Name: Lemon Bay Scallop Restoration
Project_Description: Lemon Bay is designated as the Lemon Bay Aquatic Preserve and is managed to protect and restore submerged habitats, including seagrass, fish and shellfish. Bay scallop populations declined in the 1960s, primarily due to over harvest. Recovery of bay scallop populations requires adequate sources of larvae, especially following red tide events. Over 2 million bay scallop larvae, collected from nearshore waters in the Florida Panhandle, were released into Lemon Bay over healthy seagrass beds just prior to the stage in their life cycle where they settle onto the seagrass and develop into juvenile scallops. The purpose of the larval release was to provide adequate numbers of juvenile scallops to grow to adulthood and spawn the following fall in Lemon Bay. Monitoring of adult populations and next year’s recruitment of larvae is planned. The project involved local, state and regional agencies, as well as volunteers.
Habitat_Description: Lemon Bay (approximately 7,700 acres) is located in western Charlotte and Lee Counties between the mainland and a series of barrier islands. Lemon Bay is connected to the Gulf of Mexico through Stump and Little Gasparilla Passes. It is designated as the Lemon Bay Aquatic Preserve. It is a narrow, shallow estuary with a large percent of shoreline in mangrove habitat and a moderately developed watershed. Lemon Bay supports over 3,800 acres of seagrasses including turtle grass, shoal grass and manatee grass. The submerged habitats support a great diversity of fish, shellfish, invertebrates and marine mammals including oyster, clams, shrimp, mangrove snapper, snook, dolphins and manatees. Historically, bay scallops were abundant in Lemon Bay, but populations declined dramatically after the 1960s due to primarily to overharvesting. Seagrass and water quality conditions are adequate to support bay scallop populations, but sources of larvae are limited and red tide adversely impacts fledgling populations.

Project_Description: This is a habitat restoration project at the 564 acre Matlacha Pass National Wildlife Refuge managed by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service as part of the J.N. “Ding” Darling National Wildlife Refuge. Habitat restoration activities focus on removal of non-native vegetation from the refuge islands. The habitat restoration projects improve wildlife habitat within refuge islands, as well as protect submerged seagrass habitats in the adjacent estuary. Endangered and threatened species which also benefit from the habitat restoration and protection include bald eagles and wood storks, sea turtles, and manatees. Habitat_Description: Matlacha Pass National Wildlife Refuge (564 acres) is managed by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service as a satellite refuge of J.N. "Ding" Darling National Wildlife Refuge. The refuge is located in central Lee County within the Matlacha Pass Aquatic Preserve. The refuge includes the original three small islands established as a preserve and breeding ground for native birds in 1908 plus 20 additional islands included in subsequent years, now encompassing 512 acres. The designation protects the lands from past and future development, including mining, fish camps and residential uses. The refuge islands are part of a highly productive estuary which supports a diverse array of wildlife. The islands contain two basic vegetative zones - upland sand ridges and mangroves. Several of the islands used as roosting and nesting sites for a variety of wading and water birds. The beaches and shores provide loafing, feeding, and nesting areas for migratory ducks, shorebirds, gulls, and terns. Ospreys, which are listed as a priority species in the Regional Resource Plan, can be observed nesting and feeding in Matlacha Pass area. Several endangered and threatened species benefit from the habitats described including bald eagles, wood storks, sea turtles, and manatees.

Project_Description: This project restored appropriate dune vegetation to approximately 20 acres of degraded beach dune habitat in Perdido Key, Florida, including habitat used by the federally endangered Perdido Key Beach Mouse. Project_Name: Perdido Key Sediment Placement
Project_Description:
This project partially supplemented the natural sediment budget for the Perdido Key Unit of Gulf Islands National Seashore by placing at least 400,000 cubic yards (cy) of sediment dredged from Pensacola Pass onto the Gulfside eastern half of Perdido Key. The National Park Service (NPS) worked in close coordination with U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) to do so.

Specifically, the project:
 - Re-introduced sand into the barrier-island system using a pipeline from the dredging location. The exact placement location was determined by the condition of the shoreline at the time of dredging.
 - Determined a way to facilitate National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) Section 106 compliance for all future sediment placement projects on Perdido Key. Originally the idea was to complete a 106 survey for the entire seven-mile southern shoreline of the Perdido Key Unit. Upon discussions with the Florida State Historic Preservation Office (SHPO), however, that was changed to creating a Programmatic Agreement with the SHPO for future 106 surveys at Perdido Key.

The goals of the project are to improve wildlife and plant habitat at Perdido Key and improve the ability of Perdido Key to withstand the natural erosive effects of storms. A historical sediment deficit exists in the system due to recurring maintenance dredging of the lower harbor federal navigation channel. This dredging, with offshore deposition of the sediment, has interrupted the natural westward littoral drift of sand, leading to unnaturally narrow beaches and diminished habitat, storm protection, and recreational opportunities on Perdido Key. 

Project activities included planning/design, implementation, and monitoring. Two placement events occurred: one completed in May 2022 for 181,000 cy and one completed in February 2024 for 915,666 cy. The two events were coordinated with USACE for maintenance dredging in Pensacola Pass and were partially funded by USACE, allowing DOI to place more sediment at the Perdido Key Unit than it originally hoped to.

Project_Name: Rattlesnake Bluff Road and Riverbank Restoration
Project_Description:
This project will improve water quality by mitigating the impacts of excessive sedimentation to the Yellow River and Pensacola Bay, Florida, through road stabilization and culvert replacement at priority stream crossings identified along Rattlesnake Bluff Road in Santa Rosa and Okaloosa counties. The Yellow River and Pensacola Bay are designated priority waterbodies in the State of Florida. 

Reducing sedimentation will improve water quality and also benefit estuarine-dependent water column resources, oysters, and Submerged Aquatic Vegetation (SAV), and mitigate chronic ecosystem threats such as habitat degradation and impacts to recreational use. Four priority stream crossings have been selected for restoration activities including Camp Creek, Carroll Creek, and Milligan Creek, Okaloosa County, and Wolf Creek, Santa Rosa County, Florida. Drainage system: Yellow River. Landowner: Eglin Airforce Base.

Project_Name: St Lucie County Impoundment 14C
Project_Description: Coastal wetlands are among the most biologically productive natural ecosystems on Earth. Unfortunately, on Florida’s northeast and east-central coasts, wetlands were historically considered mosquito factories, uninviting wastelands with no inherent value. For decades, the Indian River Lagoon’s wetlands were filled, ditched and diked — mostly to control mosquito populations, with little regard for the other ecological values they provided. By the 1970s, more than 40,000 acres of coastal wetlands (approximately 75 percent of the lagoonwide total) were impounded and isolated from the lagoon. Pumping water into these isolated impoundments stopped most mosquito production, but also impacted the vegetation and many wetland functions. This project is phase 2 of wetland restoration, management, and water quality improvement to an impounded swamp adjacent to the Indian River Lagoon in St. Lucie County. Prior to impoundment, the swamp was a healthy mangrove marsh. During this phase the quad pump station was completed in the dike. The pump station helps to continue restoring this impoundment area to a more natural hydrology, allowing exchange of water to the lagoon. The quality, clarity, and circulation of waters of an additional 26-acre restored wetland and of the waters of the Lagoon immediately off shore from the project area are significantly improved by the restored filtering function of the mangrove marsh and seasonal pumping of waters into the wetland. Additional phases will add educational nature trails, and information kiosks to the site.
Habitat_Description: Impounded wetlands along the eastern shore of the Indian River Lagoon in St Lucie county.

Project_Name: St. Lucie Estuary Oyster Reef Habitat Restoration Project
Project_Description:
The purpose of the St. Lucie Estuary (SLE) Oyster Reef Habitat Restoration Project is to restore historic oyster reef habitat and improve shoreline stability. By restoring approximately 2 acres of oyster reef habitat, and creating stretches of living shoreline, in the SLE, the project furthers the Estuary Restoration Act's mission to protect and restore marine and coastal habitats.  The project also furthers NOAA’s coastal resiliency objectives due to the fact that oyster reef restoration combined with living shorelines can help to protect against stresses caused by sea level rise/climate change.  

By leveraging the ERA funds with St. Lucie River Issues Team grant funds, the County was able to increase the constructed oyster reef acreage to 4.52 acres during the summer of 2013. The living shoreline component of oyster shell bags, oyster domes and saltmarsh planting was completed early summer 2014.  959 volunteers contributed 2133 hours to the living shoreline component of the project.  This project will post-restoration monitoring efforts through the fall of 2017.

Control of raccoon populations and removal of feral hogs will help restore habitat and protect natural resources on the island.

Project_Name: Telogia Creek Watershed Water Quality Improvements
Project_Description: The project will improve surface water and aquatic habitat quality in the Telogia Creek subbasin by both reducing sediment, nutrient, and pollutant loading as well as improving habitat stability and natural flow regimes. This project will be conducted in phases. Project_Description: The Nature Conservancy (TNC) and project partners built upon Acropora coral recovery and restoration work that was piloted with TNC-NOAA Community-based Habitat Restoration Grant Program (CRP) support beginning in 2004. The project capitalized on these previous efforts by maintaining a minimum of 10,000 corals in established nurseries managed by TNC and its partners, and outplanting 8,000 additional corals to degraded reefs over two years. Project_Description: The project will provide and enhance recreational opportunities at Topsail Hill Preserve State Park by constructing additional recreational access and amenities. Specifically, the project includes:  • Construction of an open-air interpretive pavilion as a waiting area for the tram that currently circulates visitors from the entrance area to the Gulf beach access and Campbell Lake; • Construction of two bike-share stations that would allow visitors to park and ride between the entrance and Gulf beach access areas with the ability to park bicycles at either end; • Construction of an additional boardwalk at the Gulf beach-use area; • Construction of a tram pavilion at the north end of the boardwalk; • Construction of a 10-fixture restroom facility at the north end of the boardwalk; • Construction of a paddle-craft launch on the north shore of Campbell Lake, which would provide recreational access to one of the park’s most significant features; • Replacement of the campground bathhouse with a 25-fixture restroom facility; • Installation of interpretive signage at the entrance and other areas to educate visitors on the restoration efforts and rare coastal dune lake ecosystem. Project_Name: Upper Florida Keys Coral Population Enhancement through Active Propagation - CRF
Project_Description: This project addressed restoration actions to help recover Acropora cervicornis (staghorn coral) and A. palmata (elkhorn coral), two coral species that are listed as “Threatened” under the Endangered Species Act.   Staghorn (9,925) and elkhorn (4,100) corals were transplanted from Coral Reef Foundation nurseries to reefs at densities and sizes that exceed what is found within the natural population.  Relatively large corals (>25cm to 45cm diameter) were grown in nurseries and transplanted to various reef sites in the Florida Keys.  Through careful hypothesis-driven monitoring, whether or not clusters and thickets that approximate pre-dieoff densities will be more resilient to existing disturbances was observed. The project also addressed developing offshore nursery techniques for three additional species of stony coral that were listed as threatened under the US Endangered Species Act after the project began (Orbicella annularis, Orbicella faveolata, and Dendrogyra cylindricus).

Project_Name: Yucca Pens Wildlife Management Unit ATV Trail Ditch Blocks
Project_Description: This is a hydrologic restoration project at the 14,577 acre Yucca Pens Wildlife Management Unit of the Babcock/Webb Wildlife Management Areas managed by the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission. Hydrologic restoration activities completed included blocking 23 ATV trail ditches with rock and installing 1 24” riser in the southeastern, as well as additional fencing and posting, in the southeastern portion of the Yucca Pens Wildlife Management Unit. The ditch blocks restored natural hydrology to over 1,000 acres of hydric and mesic pine flatwoods and tidal creeks.
Habitat_Description: The Yucca Pens Wildlife Management Unit (14,577 acres) of the Babcock/Webb Wildlife Management Area is managed by the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission. The Yucca Pens Wildlife Management Unit is located in southwestern Charlotte County and northwestern Lee County within the Charlotte Harbor watershed. The habitats include primarily hydric and mesic pine flatwoods, with some freshwater marsh and oak scrub. The habitats support a great diversity of wildlife, birds, fish and native plants including Florida black bear, bob cat, coyote, otter, eagle, osprey, wild turkeys, great blue heron, mosquitofish and killifish, as well as invasive exotic feral hogs. There are moderate areas of invasive exotic vegetation including Brazilian pepper, Australian pine, Melaleuca, cogongrass, and old world climbing fern. Illegal ATV use throughout the Yucca Pens Wildlife Management Unit created extensive trails which act as artificial ditches and caused widespread hydrologic changes from natural sheet flow to channelized flow. The ATV trails are being reduced through fencing, posting and hydrologic restoration activities.

tier1_dup_key: 26.72879 -81.97792 Yucca Pens Wildlife Management Unit ATV Trail Ditch Blocks This is a hydrologic restoration project at the 14,577 acre Yucca Pens Wildlife Management Unit of the Babcock/Webb Wildlife Management Areas managed by the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission. Hydrologic restoration activities completed included blocking 23 ATV trail ditches with rock and installing 1 24” riser in the southeastern, as well as additional fencing and posting, in the southeastern portion of the Yucca Pens Wildlife Management Unit. The ditch blocks restored natural hydrology to over 1,000 acres of hydric and mesic pine flatwoods and tidal creeks.
